newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - T-bond vols soft, April expires quietly.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - T-bond vols soft, April expires quietly.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options softened as underlying bond prices hovered in very narrow ranges and weekend time-decay set in, dealers said.
"A lot of people taking positions have already done so and they're just waiting for the Tuesday meeting (of the Federal Open Market Committee)," said a brokerage trader at CBOT.

April T-bond futures options on the Chicago Board of Trade expired without causing noticeable turbulence as June futures drifted between the 108 and 109 strikes, the center of open-interest concentration.
Traders said T-bond options have had a notorious tendency to expire where the highest number of contracts expire worthless.

The just out-of-the-money April 108 puts had the highest open interest among puts with 22,200 contracts at the end of Thursday's business, while 107 and 109 puts each had around 12,000. April 110, 111 and 112 calls -- all out-of-the-money -- had the highest open interest on the call side with around 20,000 contracts each.
Implied volatilities for CBOT May and June T-bond options lost about 0.2 point to 9.1 and 9.2 percent respectively.

Traders said there was still enough uncertainty left to keep volatilities from sliding sharply, even though the market already generally anticipated that the Federal Reserve would tighten credit at Tuesday's FOMC meeting after Fed chairman Alan Greenspan's hawkish remarks on Thursday.
"We were hoping to get some kind of an indication from Greenspan yesterday," the CBOT trader said. "I think we did, but it's not for sure yet. You can't keep keep getting short."
Despite growing optimism that the worst is over, some traders warned that the rapid yield-curve flattening since Thursday could eventually reverse, depressing the bond market.

"It (curve-flattening) seems to be the right thing, given the market's perception that we're getting a tightening and that's going to be it," said a Eurodollar trader for an investment bank at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.
"But the curve could steepen back out once we actually get a tightening," he noted. "The idea of a pre-emptive strike is nice but once we get one the market could start reacting differently."
Indeed, Greenspan himself said on Thursday that the effect of a tightening on inflation might not be felt for a while even if the FOMC elected to raise rates at Tuesday's meeting.

In Eurodollars, mid-curve options -- options expiring in 1997 but priced from 1998 futures -- saw the inversion in their volatility curve steepen as lingering nervousness supported gamma-rich shorter maturities.
Implied volatilities for short-April and short-May options gained a few tenths to 18.0 and 16.7 percent, respectively.

The volatility curve for the plain front-month Eurodollar futures options were softer as their underlying futures were relatively narrow-ranged due to the gravity of the cash deposit rate. June, September and December Eurodollar futures volatilities stood at 9.6, 12.2 and 13.6 percent respectively.
